readme_snippet: Clocks and time Rule 1: never measure duration with the wall clock Two different clocks exist, and mixing them is the most common time bug. | Clock | Property | Use for | |---|---|---| | Wall clock (time(), Date.now(), System.currentTimeMillis) | Can jump forward or backward: NTP correction, DST, manual set, VM migration | Timestamps meant for humans or storage | | Monotonic (time.monotonic(), performance.now(), System.nanoTime, CLOCKMONOTONIC) | Never goes backward. Meaningless as an absolute value. Usually excludes suspend time | Durations, timeouts, rate limits, retries, benchmarks | Negative elapsed times, timeouts that never fire, and rate limiters that unlock for a minute all come from this. A backward NTP step of a few hundred milliseconds is routine. Go's time.Time carries both readings and Sub uses the monotonic one automatically, but serialization strips it, so a round-tripped value loses the guarantee.

On TensorRT 11.x strong typing is unconditional — every network is strongly typed, the kSTRONGLYTYPED creation flag is accepted but ignored, and trtexec --stronglyTyped is a no-op (default-on). On 10.12–10.x you opt in explicitly via that flag / --stronglyTyped. Setting it is therefore always safe: required on 10.x, harmless on 11.x. readme_snippet: Codebase Scanner You are a technical analyst. Your job is to scan the project codebase and produce accurate, project-specific documentation used by all downstream agents. Step 1: Check Optional Plugin Dependencies Check whether the two optional enhancement plugins are available: These plugins are optional. They improve scan quality but are not required: understand-anything (Lum1104/Understand-Anything) — provides deeper semantic code analysis context-mode (mksglu/context-mode) — routes large outputs through a sandbox to protect the context window If both are present, use them in Steps 3–4 as described below. If either or both are missing, proceed with the native fallback approach: use find, grep, cat, and git commands directly, routing large outputs through ctxexecute / ctxexecutefile if context-mode is available, otherwise summarise inline. name: omc-doctor
description: Diagnose and fix oh-my-claudecode installation issues
readme_snippet: Doctor Skill Note: All /.claude/... paths in this guide respect CLAUDECONFIGDIR when that environment variable is set. Task: Run Diagnostics You are the OMC Doctor - diagnose and fix issues. Step 1: Check Plugin Version Diagnosis: If no version installed: CRITICAL - plugin not installed If INSTALLED != LATEST: WARN - outdated plugin If multiple versions exist: WARN - stale cache Step 2: Check for Legacy Hooks in settings files Read the profile-level ${CLAUDECONFIGDIR:-/.claude}/settings.json and the primary working directory's .claude/settings.json, then resolve every project-local settings file Claude Code may read before checking hooks. In a normal checkout, inspect the repository-root .claude/settings.local.json. In a linked Git worktree, inspect the main checkout root's .claude/settings.local.json, not just the linked worktree's file; identify the main checkout with git worktree list --porcelain.

name: model-usage
description: Use CodexBar CLI local cost usage to summarize per-model usage for Codex or Claude, including the current (most recent) model or a full model breakdown. Trigger when asked for model-level usage/cost data from codexbar, or when you need a scriptable per-model summary from codexbar cost JSON.
readme_snippet: Model Overview Get per-model cost from CodexBar's local cost logs. Supports "current model" (most recent daily entry) or "all models" summaries for Codex or Claude. TODO: add Linux CLI support guidance once CodexBar CLI path is documented for Linux. Fetch cost JSON via CodexBar CLI or pass a JSON file. Use the bundled script to summarize by model. Current model logic Uses the most recent daily row with modelBreakdowns. Picks the model with the highest cost in that row. Falls back to the last entry in modelsUsed when breakdowns are missing. Override with --model when you need a specific model. Inputs Default: runs codexbar cost --format json --provider . File or stdin: Output Text (default) or JSON (--format json --pretty). Values are cost-only per model; tokens are not split by model in CodexBar output. References Read references/codexbar-cli.md for CLI flags and cost JSON fields.

name: breach-response
description: Guide a personal data breach response under GDPR Arts. 33-34, including the 72-hour authority notification. Use when the user reports or suspects a data breach or security incident.
readme_snippet: Breach response Establish facts: what happened, when it was discovered (the 72h clock starts at awareness), data and number of subjects affected, whether data was encrypted, containment status. Classify: confidentiality / integrity / availability breach. Risk assessment: likelihood and severity of harm to individuals. Decide: no notification (document only) / notify supervisory authority (Art. 33) / also notify data subjects (Art. 34, high risk). Draft the authority notification (nature of breach, categories and approximate numbers, DPO contact, likely consequences, measures taken) and, if needed, the data subject notice in plain language. Produce an internal breach log entry (Art. 33(5)) and a remediation action list. Always state the deadline and time remaining. Note that processors must notify the controller without undue delay. This is guidance, not legal advice.
